name: Purple Shamrock
variety: Species; leaf-color forms and cultivars not specified
summary: A South American rhizomatous perennial grown as a container ornamental for its trifoliate leaves, which fold at night. NC State Extension documents rhizome division as a propagation route; seed is also listed, but no germination protocol is established here.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Oxalis triangularis. NC State Extension calls it purple shamrock and notes Oxalis regnellii as a previous name; the profile represents the species, not one of the named cultivars listed by the extension source.

cultivation.short: Container ornamental with a seasonal dormancy pattern
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes well-drained potting mix and full sun to partial shade in its regional guidance. It reports the plant may go dormant when conditions are hot or dry and recommends reducing watering while dormant; this is not an indoor grow-light tier.

growth.short: Rhizomatous perennial with leaves that fold at night
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes a herbaceous perennial arising from rhizomes with trifoliate leaves that close at night or when disturbed. The source lists multiple named cultivars and forms; no single leaf color or cultivar is assigned to this species-level entry.

maintenance.short: Reduce watering during dormancy; divide rhizomes to propagate
maintenance.guidance: NC State Extension describes reducing watering when the plant enters dormancy and says rhizome division or detached scale leaves can produce new plants. Its source also lists seed as a propagation strategy, but does not provide a sowing or germination protocol.

problems.short: No serious insect or disease problems are reported
problems.guidance: NC State Extension reports no serious insect or disease problems for this species. Its leaves normally close at night or when disturbed, and seasonal dormancy may occur; these documented behaviors alone are not signs of disease.

safety.short: Edibility is qualified; all parts have toxic potential
safety.guidance: NC State Extension lists leaves and flowers as edible only in moderation and also warns that all parts have toxic potential, with serious effects generally associated with large ingestions. This is not a serving recommendation or a claim of unrestricted food safety.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The extension source describes container and garden culture, not hydroponic production.

evidence.note: NC State describes the species as growing from rhizomes; this does not establish fit for a specific machine.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light classification.

name: Arrowhead Plant
summary: A tropical evergreen aroid commonly grown indoors for arrow-shaped juvenile foliage. NC State Extension documents cuttings, layering and division, and notes that leaf shape changes as the plant matures.

identity.guidance: Kew's Plants of the World Online lists Syngonium podophyllum within the accepted genus. NC State Extension identifies this species as American evergreen and arrowhead plant; named cultivar traits are not assigned here.

cultivation.short: Bright shade, warmth and humidity suit indoor growth
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension recommends a warm, humid location and avoiding full sun because direct light can burn or bleach foliage. These are houseplant/landscape recommendations; they do not prove compatibility with a hydroponic appliance.

growth.short: Young plants are bushy; mature growth becomes vine-like
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes a shrub-like juvenile form that becomes climbing or trailing with age, with leaves changing from arrow-shaped to more divided adult forms. Its source includes several named cultivars; this record is species-level only.

maintenance.short: Prune stems to retain a bushier juvenile form
maintenance.guidance: Cutting stems as they begin to develop can retain the arrowhead foliage and a more shrub-like habit. NC State Extension says repotting every few years and trimming the root system can help keep the plant manageable. It also lists division, layering and stem cuttings as propagation routes; this is not a cultivar-specific pruning calendar.

problems.short: Watch for pests, bacterial leaf spots and soft rot
problems.guidance: NC State Extension lists aphids, mealybugs and spider mites, as well as bacterial leaf spots and soft rot. Leaf spots or soft rot are possible disease signs; the source does not provide a diagnosis from appearance alone. This is a monitoring list, not a claim that every plant will develop them or that the identity has resistance traits.

safety.short: The species contains calcium oxalate crystals and is toxic if chewed
safety.guidance: NC State Extension classifies this species as poisonous and identifies calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing can cause oral irritation, pain or swelling, drooling, vomiting, or difficulty swallowing; sap can also irritate skin. The source documents these hazards but does not provide exposure-treatment guidance.

evidence.note: The species becomes vine-like with age; this alone does not establish system fit.

name: Baby Rubber Plant
summary: A compact tropical evergreen houseplant with glossy, fleshy, oval leaves. NC State Extension recommends bright indirect light and cautions that overwatering can yellow leaves and lead to root rot; leaf and stem cuttings are documented propagation methods.

identity.guidance: World Flora Online lists Peperomia obtusifolia as a botanical species in Piperaceae. NC State Extension describes the oval-leaf peperomia and notes that other cultivars exist; this identity does not specify a variegated cultivar.

cultivation.short: Bright indirect light; avoid persistently wet or very dry soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes bright indirect light, notes that non-variegated forms can tolerate lower light for several months, and warns against wet or very dry soil. This is houseplant guidance and does not define a grow-light tier or hydroponic suitability.

growth.short: Erect, bushy shrub with glossy cupped leaves
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes an erect, bushy herbaceous shrub with glossy cupped leaves, distinct branched stems and cream-colored flower spikes. Its plant profile gives a broad 6-inch-to-2-foot height and width range; this reflects the source's houseplant context, not a guaranteed size in a controlled system. The page lists several cultivars, but no cultivar-specific color or dimensions are applied here.

propagation.short: Leaf or stem cuttings; a leaf-petiole method is documented for peperomias
propagation.guidance: NC State Extension lists leaf and stem cuttings for Peperomia obtusifolia. Iowa State's general houseplant guide identifies peperomias as suitable for leaf-petiole propagation: select a firm leaf, leave about 1–1½ inches of petiole, place it in a moist, airy rooting medium, and keep it warm, humid, and in bright indirect light. Iowa State reports roots in about 3–4 weeks and plantlets in 6–8 weeks for this method overall; those are group-level estimates, not a Peperomia obtusifolia timetable or guarantee. The method is vegetative and does not imply seed-starting instructions.

problems.short: Overwatering can yellow leaves and contribute to root rot
problems.guidance: NC State Extension identifies overwatering as a major problem and lists yellowing and root rot as possible outcomes; it also recommends monitoring for mealybugs, spider mites and whiteflies. This is risk guidance, not a diagnosis of an individual plant.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Houseplant and potting-mix guidance does not establish production in a hydroponic system.

evidence.note: The extension source describes an erect, bushy houseplant; compactness does not establish machine compatibility.

height.reason: The selected evidence does not establish controlled-system mature height for this identity.

light.reason: Outdoor and indoor ambient-light descriptions are not a grow-light intensity classification.

name: Satin Pothos
summary: A tropical climbing aroid with silver-mottled foliage, often grown as a trailing houseplant. NC State Extension documents stem cuttings and describes bright indirect indoor light; no universal hydroponic compatibility is inferred.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Scindapsus pictus. NC State Extension lists satin pothos and silver pothos as common names and Scindapsus argyraeus among previously used names; this entry does not select one of the named cultivars on the page.

cultivation.short: Bright indirect light, drained soil, and 65–85°F (about 18–29°C)
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes bright indirect light, moist, well-drained potting soil and a 65–85°F (about 18–29°C) range for houseplant use; it notes intolerance of direct sunlight and cool air. These conditions do not establish nutrient solution targets or hydroponic system compatibility.

growth.short: Climbing or trailing vine; indoor height is typically 1.5–3 feet
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes a tropical evergreen vine that may climb on support or trail from a hanging container; juvenile leaves are silver-mottled and adult leaves may become lobed. In the source's houseplant context it gives a typical indoor height of 1.5–3 feet. Indoor flowering is uncommon; the longer native-vine dimensions are not applied to this container-grown record.

maintenance.short: Pinch stems to keep the plant tidy; stem cuttings propagate it
maintenance.guidance: NC State Extension says pinching stems helps keep the plant tidy and documents stem cuttings as a propagation method. This does not claim a seed protocol or cultivar-specific pruning response.

problems.short: Poor drainage can contribute to root rot
problems.guidance: NC State Extension notes root rot risk in poorly drained or wet soil and says yellow leaves may signal overwatering while curling may indicate underwatering. These are possible signs, not definitive diagnoses.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source supports houseplant potting culture, not hydroponic production.

evidence.note: Climbing and trailing habit is documented; it does not establish machine fit.

height.reason: The source gives both indoor and native vine context; no controlled-system mature height is selected.

name: Chinese Money Plant
summary: A compact Chinese evergreen perennial houseplant with round, peltate leaves and a clumping habit. NC State Extension documents propagation by offsets and stem cuttings during active growth; this profile does not imply seed availability.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Pilea peperomioides in Urticaceae. NC State Extension lists Chinese money plant, coin plant and pancake plant as common names; no cultivar is specified.

cultivation.short: Bright indirect light and evenly moist, well-drained mix
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes bright indirect sunlight, moist well-drained potting mix and tolerance of average household humidity; it recommends avoiding cold drafts and heat sources. Its page presents houseplant care, not a controlled grow-light setting or hydroponic recipe.

growth.short: Compact, erect and clumping, with circular peltate leaves
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes a compact, erect, clumping perennial with fleshy circular leaves whose long stems attach at the center. Its houseplant profile gives a height and width of about 8–12 inches; these dimensions are not guarantees for a controlled system or every container.

flowering.short: Small white-to-pink spikes may appear, but houseplants rarely flower
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension describes small white-to-pinkish flowers on tall spikes and notes that houseplants rarely flower. A lack of flowers is therefore normal in the indoor setting; no bloom schedule or environmental trigger is established by this source.

maintenance.short: Separate offsets or use stem cuttings in active growth
maintenance.guidance: NC State Extension documents offsets or pups and stem cuttings, with propagation best during spring or early summer active growth. This is vegetative propagation guidance; no seed germination protocol is provided.

problems.short: Avoid overwatering and wet foliage; monitor common houseplant pests
problems.guidance: NC State Extension warns that overwatering can lead to root rot and lists spider mites, mealybugs, fungus gnats and scale for monitoring. It says wet foliage can result in leaf spots and leggy growth can result from inadequate light; these are possible issues rather than a diagnosis.
